## Active

### D-926 — The log viewer reads lukaot records through one accessor module

> _2026-11-20 · tools/blong-log · active_

The viewer reads a record the way lukaot writes it, and the shape is not the pino one it was built
for: the service is `service`, the identity an operator filters by is `fields.context` (a port's
`srv.db`, a component's class name), the declared identifier is `signal` (promoted to the top level
for a sink that indexes, and still in `fields`), and a capture carries
`fields.capture`/`shape`/`rung` beside the fields its shape rendered, with the payload in
`fields.payload`. One module, `src/record.ts`, holds every accessor and is imported by the server,
the buffer and the client alike, so the spelling is decided once instead of in three `??` chains.

The viewer changed with it: the `Where` column shows service and context, a `Signal` column carries
the declared identifier and marks the rows that hold a capture, and the filters gained `signal` and
`capture` end to end — the toolbar, the REST query, the WebSocket match and the circular buffer,
which had its own copy of the filter logic and would otherwise have answered a different question
from the socket. `name` still addresses the port, falling back to the service, because a reader who
typed `gateway` meant where the line came from.

Two tautologies were removed rather than carried over: the capture panel repeated the identifier and
the shape the row already showed, and the params panel repeated the signal. What is left in a
capture's header is what only the capture knows — the rung, the direction, the size, the label.

### D-927 — A tcp capture is drawn as a hex dump with its ASCII computed from the bytes

> _2026-11-20 · tools/blong-log · active_

A frame is drawn the way a hex editor draws it: an offset column, sixteen bytes a row with a gap
between the halves, and the bytes' ASCII beside them. Both columns come from the record's hex
payload — the ASCII is computed in the viewer rather than read from `fields.ascii`, because the
shape writes that only for the first preview bytes at the `hex` rung while the payload carries every
byte, so deriving it is both complete and free. A byte the masker withheld arrives as `00` and reads
as `.`, which is the honest picture: the value is gone, not hidden.

The grain is what makes the two columns worth the width: an ISO 8583 request shows its MTI as `0200`
in the ASCII column and its bitmap as dots, and a reader can tell a text protocol from a binary one
without decoding anything. Sixteen per row because that is what every dump tool a developer has used
does; the header row is built from the same cell widths as the data so a column cannot drift.

A payload that is not hex yields no rows and says so rather than drawing a wrong picture — `hexDump`
answers an empty list for a sentence, an odd digit count or a non-hex character, and the panel shows
the honest sentence instead.

### D-928 — The producer is a lukaot writer, and the addresses come from the request

> _2026-11-20 · tools/blong-log · active_

The viewer's producer is a lukaot **writer**, not a pino transport. The framework stopped writing
through pino when the vocabulary landed, so the pipeline the viewer was built for no longer existed:
`blong-log` served its API and had nothing to serve. `createUdpWriter` installs with `setWriter` and
ships the **record** — lukaot hands a destination the rendered line and the record, and a viewer
given only the line could show the sentence but none of the fields a capture row draws. The wire
format is unchanged (a JSON array of records split across packets with a 12-byte batch header), so
nothing in the server learned about pino or about lukaot; `src/packets.ts` now holds the one
definition both producers use.

Two defects surfaced while proving the loop and are fixed with it. The package had no
`public/index.html` at all, so `/` answered 404 in every environment — a viewer nobody could open;
the shell is now a source file beside the bundle the build writes. And its local imports used `.js`
specifiers, which only the tap loader resolves, so `node src/cli.ts` could not start the documented
local run; they are `.ts`/`.tsx` now, which is the repository's convention anyway.

`/api/config` also stopped trusting the address the server bound to: it is derived from the request
(`x-forwarded-host`/`x-forwarded-proto`, else the request's host and encryption), because a page
reached through a forwarded port or an ingress must be told where _it_ can reach the API. That is
the first piece a deployment needs, and it costs nothing when the viewer is visited directly.
